title: He that dwelleth (Psalm 90 [91])
hook: under his wings, and angels to keep thee in all thy ways

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prayer of Moses: teach us to number our days. Your line was number your days. Today closes the week, under wings.

If you grew up Catholic, there may have been a small picture over your bed: two children crossing a rickety bridge over a gorge at night, planks broken, water rushing below, and behind them, huge and gentle, an angel with its wings spread, keeping them from falling. Sentimental, maybe. But the idea behind it is old and serious, and a lot of it comes from one psalm, a psalm the devil himself once quoted.
screen: `TWO CHILDREN ON A BROKEN BRIDGE.` → `AN ANGEL BEHIND THEM.` → `A PSALM THE DEVIL QUOTED.`

segments.voice: Psalm 90 in the Douay, 91 in most Bibles: "He that dwelleth in the aid of the most High, shall abide under the protection of the God of Jacob." Then a mother bird: "He will overshadow thee with his shoulders: and under his wings thou shalt trust." Then the fears: the terror of the night, the arrow that flies by day, the thing that walks about in the dark, the noonday devil. And then: "For he hath given his angels charge over thee; to keep thee in all thy ways. In their hands they shall bear thee up: lest thou dash thy foot against a stone." Here's where the devil comes in. In the desert, Matthew says, the tempter took Jesus to the top of the Temple, quoted these lines, and said: jump. The angels will catch you. Scripture, used as bait. Jesus answered with other scripture: "Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." The psalm is a promise of care, not a dare. From this psalm, and from Jesus's words that children's angels always see the face of his Father in heaven, the Church draws its teaching on guardian angels. The Catechism says that beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd, and that human life, from its beginning until death, is surrounded by the angels' care. Catholics keep a feast of the guardian angels on October 2, and there's a short traditional prayer to one's angel, the kind children learn by heart. It's also the Church's Sunday night psalm, at Compline. The week ran from a thirsty deer to be still, a clean heart, a morning thirst, a sparrow's home and numbered days, and ends here: under his wings.
screen: `UNDER HIS WINGS THOU SHALT TRUST.` · `ANGELS TO KEEP THEE.` · `THE DEVIL QUOTES IT: JUMP.` · `A GUARDIAN FROM CHILDHOOD.`

segments.voice: Think of your own rickety bridge this week, whatever feels unsteady, and something large and gentle behind you, wings open, not stopping you from walking, just keeping you from falling. If you pray, speak to your guardian angel in your own words, or with the traditional prayer to the guardian angel; if you don't, rest in the picture of being kept.
Guardian angel. The angel Catholics believe stands beside each believer, as protector and shepherd, from the beginning of life until death. Today's word.
Your line: under his wings. The bridge is still yours to walk. A week of psalms, done.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 90 [91] at Night Prayer on Sundays and on the first Sunday of Lent, when the Gospel tells of the temptation in the desert; some pray daily to their guardian angel, and the Church keeps the feast of the Guardian Angels on October 2.

what it means: the Church's teaching that each believer is kept by an angel, drawn from Psalm 90 and the words of Jesus.
what a scholar hears: angel is Greek angelos, messenger; the psalm's promise was quoted by the tempter in Matthew 4, and Jesus answered with Deuteronomy.

notes: Douay Psalm 90:1, 4, 11–12 and Matthew 4:7 wording: confirm against a Challoner edition.
The 'guardian angel on the bridge' picture is a well-known 19th/20th-century devotional print; described generically.
CCC 336 (quoting Basil): beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd; human life from infancy to death surrounded by their care. Paraphrased.
Psalm 91 at Night Prayer after Evening Prayer II of Sunday; responsorial psalm on the First Sunday of Lent (Year C). Confirm.
Practice mentions 'the traditional prayer' (Angele Dei / Angel of God) without quoting it.
